short_description: The family tablet takes a nap, nightcap and all. So Ada builds, splashes, blasts off and bakes. A funny, warm read-aloud for ages 3–7.
long_description:
Shhh… the tablet is sleeping. So what shall we do today?

On Saturday morning, Ada zooms downstairs to find the family tablet, and finds it wearing a nightcap and snoring a tiny 'zzz-bip'. It worked hard all week, Papa explains, and today it gets to rest. So Ada and her dog Biscuit fill the day themselves. They build a block tower (CRASH!), splash through every puddle, turn a big empty box into a rocket, flip pancakes with Papa and find the perfect book at the library. At bedtime, everybody sleeps. In the morning, Ada can't wait to tell the tablet all about it.

The Day the Tablet Slept is a warm, funny picture book with a repeated refrain that children soon join in on, short read-aloud pages and bold, full-bleed illustrations on every spread. The tablet is never the bad guy. It just takes a day off, and the story shows how much fun a day of play can be.

The last page has 'Talk about it' questions for grown-ups: easy prompts that turn one reading into a real back-and-forth conversation, plus simple ideas for planning your own 'tablet sleeps' day.

For ages 3–7. A lovely pick for bedtime, family reading, classrooms, libraries and gifts.
bullets: A warm, funny story for ages 3–7 about a family tablet that takes a well-earned nap, with no shame, lectures or villains
A repeated read-aloud refrain ('Shhh… the tablet is sleeping. So what shall we do today?') that children soon join in on
Bold, full-bleed flat illustrations on every spread, with an inclusive cast and a lovable dog named Biscuit to spot
Everyday play ideas kids can copy: blocks, puddle jumping, a cardboard-box rocket, cooking with a grown-up, a library visit and a bedtime story
Ends with 'Talk about it' questions for grown-ups and simple ways to plan your own play day together

compliance_notes: No health or medical claims: the book is a story plus parent-education prompts and does not claim to treat, prevent or diagnose anything. Not presented as written by a speech-language pathologist. No medical-condition language and no research citations. No trademarked program names; the grown-up tips use plain words (pause and wait, say what you see, repeat and add one word, follow their lead). No real brands, logos, devices, apps, schools or products: the tablet is a generic, unbranded character, and the copyright page says it is not based on any real product. Zero-shame tone: the tablet is never a villain; it simply rests and is welcomed back in the morning. Child safety: puddle play, cooking (the grown-up handles the stove and pan) and box-building are shown with a grown-up nearby, and the copyright and Talk pages both say these are best with a grown-up close by; no choking-hazard foods or balloons appear.
